idiom_name: ConfigFactory.load() + config.getBoolean at the toggle point
implementation_notes: ConfigFactory.load() gives the router its state through a documented merge order - system properties over application.conf over reference.conf - so a flag is a path lookup (config.getBoolean("features.new-checkout")) that is resolved once at wiring time and can be overridden per environment with -Dconfig.file or a system property without touching the code. The Config object is passed to the components that need it (or bound into a case class by a wrapper library), so the toggle point reads a typed boolean rather than the environment, and the whole configuration is reviewable as one file. The classic router is still justified when a flag needs per-request context; a Config lookup has no notion of a user.
pitfalls: ConfigFactory.load() returns a cached singleton: changing a system property after the first load has no effect until invalidateCaches() is called.

The reported merge order is per key, not per file: a reference.conf default can shadow an application.conf value if the precedence is misread, and HOCON includes can make the effective value hard to find.
A getBoolean on a missing path throws ConfigException.Missing, so an absent flag fails the request rather than defaulting off unless the key is declared in reference.conf.

variants.name: Injected () => Boolean decision instead of a config object
variants.implementation_notes: The library-free Scala form: the wiring layer reads whatever it likes (sys.props, a Config, a database, a feature service) and hands the component a function - () => Boolean or a small trait FeatureDecisions - so the class under test is constructed with () => true and the configuration library never appears in business code. This is the idiomatic form in code that already passes dependencies as functions, and it scales down gracefully: no HOCON file, no Config dependency, no cache semantics to reason about. It scales up badly, because nothing records who is allowed to flip what and no targeting context exists.
pitfalls: A () => Boolean re-reads system properties on every call, which makes a typo in the property name fail silently (absent means off) instead of at start-up.
Without a shared configuration object there is no single place to see the current flag state; the defaults live scattered across the wiring code.
